name: Emeka Chen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. What does a normal workday look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead percussion in a municipal theatre, play the kettle drums, record cue patterns and teach two young drummers. I have a master's degree in music and thirty years of paid pits behind me. The scene I enjoy is one soft roll holding a whole room quiet before the curtain lifts.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How does the theatre schedule work at home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm 58, my partner has regular shifts in a bakery and our children are grown. We rent and have four months of expenses saved. My pay is ordinary for a senior musician and some theatres are close enough for the late bus, though no principal drum post is open to me now. I use AI daily to draft cue charts, the maps of when drums enter, then check each bar against the conductor's signed score.

I'd say a **kettle drum** still responds to an actor.

The **booked show run** and lessons should hold in mild AI.

Check **AI cue charts** against signed scores and save a fifth of extra cleared festival fees after essentials.
feel: I feel **calm** while paid shows and household wages hold.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the theatre that faster cue charts help if the paid rehearsal is still printed beside the scene. A kettle drum has to answer a live actor, not a clock.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Four months saved and my partner's bakery wage cover one delayed pit fee. The current show is booked, so I expect mild AI to leave most of my playing and lessons alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week I'll confirm the next seven paid shows and my two pupils, and request written cancellation pay. In the first year of this mild change I'll keep checking daily AI cue charts against the signed score and save a fifth of any extra cleared festival fee after rent, food and drum-head repairs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm while the show run pays. A late cheque would irritate me, but it would not empty the rent account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happened at the stage door?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A stage door failed last autumn and one show moved. We received the rehearsal fee but waited for the replacement performance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do you check a cue chart?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I tap the cue on a practice pad before marking an AI chart as finished. A neat bar line can still put the drum before the actor's word.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the theatre whether generated cue patterns will replace my paid short recordings. I'd ask for written live roll and setup fees before the next production is signed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Those short recordings bring about one sixth of my own pay. If the theatre buys fewer, four months saved gives time to ask for more paid hands-on work, but an empty recording slot is still a lost fee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I'll count twelve cue invoices and ask for a paid demonstration of a new AI timing checker, which flags misplaced drum hits, from a sound engineer. In the first year I'll test only my own nameless drum take under a theatre-funded licence permitting paid use and approved local storage, outside booked calls; I'll play each marked bar against the original and stop a wrong hit or a file leaving the theatre.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about a realistic drop in my cue pay. A tidy beat is not a signed show.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use cast or pupil audio?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I would not put an actor's voice or a pupil's drumming into the trial. Their recordings need written permission and a storage rule before any use.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who pays for the demonstration?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The theatre must pay the engineer and licence without replacing a booked pit call. If it will not, I can mark the take by ear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the theatre that thinking AGI by 2028 could make cue patterns before a robot plays a drum. Playing robots follow around 2031, so our live pit calls need signing now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect the cue orders to end in 2028, costing a sixth of my pay. Live shows might also be cut, but a robot-free 2028 does not mean the theatre has already cancelled them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week I'll total cue income, seek signed paid pit dates and request actual pension statements before considering a stop at 60. In the first year after 2028, if live shows also fall, I'll seek a posted paid principal-percussion role only if my master's degree and section-leading experience qualify, live human tuning and cue-playing duties are paid, and written net pay after travel replaces lost fees and late buses run; I'll keep current pit calls and pupils until a suitable signed offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about the expected sixth of my income disappearing, while four months saved and nearby theatres give a search window. I would be alarmed if live shows collapsed too, but that is not what our current run says.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is another principal role open now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No other principal drum role is posted to me now. I would read actual paid hours, score demands and the last bus before applying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could you stop at 60?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I have not checked the pension amount. Four months saved do not tell me whether a pension could pay years of rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ordinary software may cut short cue orders before 2031. My live setup takes care and time, but I will not call it a new wage unless the theatre buys those hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Next season I'll propose a written two-year contract with paid drum setup, live cue watching and cancellation fees, showing the manager what the last six productions required. In the first year after 2031, if recorded cues end, I'll keep only signed paid pit and pupil work and use the theatre's checker on my own nameless drum take only with theatre-funded paid-use licence, approved local storage, a paid engineer lesson outside booked calls, manual play-through and stop rules for wrong cues or leakage; if live calls also fall, I'll seek a posted paid principal-percussion role only if my master's, leadership and score range qualify, live human tuning and cue-playing duties are paid, and written net pay after travel replaces lost fees and late buses run, keeping current work until a suitable signed offer.

transcript.speaker: persona

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, the manager has not agreed to those setup hours. I will budget only the signed paid calls already on the production sheet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would stop the AI trial?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would play every AI-marked cue myself before it reaches the band. A wrong note or a file leaving approved storage ends that trial.

transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my grown children ten years to AGI by 2036 lets us read real pension figures and paid theatre calls. Drum-playing robots follow around 2039, but the rent bill comes every month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 68 I may still need pit and teaching fees. Four months saved now and a pension I have not checked do not name a safe stopping date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'll request actual pension statements and a written two-year paid-show plan, then save a fifth of each extra cleared festival fee after rent, food and drum-head repairs toward six months of expenses. In the first year after 2036 I'll keep paid pit and pupil work while booked; if live pay falls and pension figures leave a gap, I'll seek a posted paid principal-percussion role only if my master's, leadership and score ability qualify, live human tuning and cue-playing duties are paid, and written net pay after travel replaces lost fees and late buses run, keeping current work until a suitable signed offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about pay that far away while the current run and four months saved give some ground. I will slow down only after reading a real pension amount beside signed fees.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if no extra festival set pays?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No extra festival set means no extra fee to save. I won't take food money to make six months show in an account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Have you checked pension figures?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, we do not have pension statements yet. I would check actual payable figures against our regular bills before leaving a paid call.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because cue fees could end before I know whether paid pit calls hold. Signed theatre dates, actual pension figures and a posted qualified principal role with written net pay after travel would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who is paid to tune the drum when a cue file is perfect. A neat cue chart cannot tighten a kettle drum head before the curtain.

headlineQuote: A neat cue chart cannot tighten a kettle drum head before the curtain.
portrait: Emeka is a **58-year-old senior percussion lead** with a music master's degree, partner and grown children.
His **typical pay**, four-month reserve and some local theatres cushion smaller cue-fee losses.
He uses **AI daily** for charts and learns a new checker only through paid safe trials on owned material.
He seeks **paid live setup hours** and verified pension figures before reducing work.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could end Emeka's smaller recorded-cue fees before live calls are certain.
whatWouldHelp: **Signed pit dates**, actual pension figures and posted qualifying principal work with written after-travel replacement pay would help.
